marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q001.takeaway: Leptomeninges are the arachnoid and pia mater; dura is pachymeninx.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q001.displayText: Leptomeninges are the arachnoid mater and pia mater. The dura mater is the pachymeninx. The source also notes that meningeal enhancement may occur in meningitis, encephalitis, tumors/metastases, inflammatory vasculitis and after seizures, trauma or surgery.

rationales.a: The dura is not a leptomeninx; including it adds the pachymeninx to the affected leptomeningeal layers.
rationales.c: This omits pia, one of the two leptomeninges involved by leptomeningeal disease.
rationales.d: This omits arachnoid, the other affected leptomeninx.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q002.takeaway: Only the endosteal dural layer contains osteoblasts; both dural layers contain fibroblasts.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q002.displayText: Both endosteal and meningeal dural layers contain fibroblasts, but only the endosteal layer contains osteoblasts. Dural venous sinuses lie between the two layers. The meningeal layer forms the dural partitions: falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli and diaphragma sellae.

rationales.a: The endosteal layer is continuous with skull periosteum, so this statement is true.
rationales.b: The meningeal dura forms partitions such as falx and tentorium; it does not divide the cavity into freely communicating spaces.
rationales.c: Dural venous sinuses lie between the endosteal and meningeal dural layers, so this is true.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q003.takeaway: Falx cerebri contains the straight sinus along its attachment to the tentorium.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q003.displayText: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the falx cerebri. Falx cerebri separates the two cerebral hemispheres; its upper fixed margin contains the superior sagittal sinus, its lower free margin the inferior sagittal sinus, and its attachment to tentorium cerebelli contains the straight sinus. Tentorium separates cerebellum from occipital lobes; falx cerebelli separates cerebellar hemispheres and contains the occipital sinus.

rationales.a: Tentorium cerebelli separates cerebellum from occipital cerebrum; that is not the falx cerebri.
rationales.b: The occipital sinus is contained in falx cerebelli, not the falx cerebri.
rationales.d: Falx cerebelli separates the cerebellar hemispheres; falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q004.takeaway: Cranial dura is supplied by trigeminal branches, upper cervical nerves and sympathetic fibers, not facial nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q004.displayText: The marked structure is cranial dura mater. It is innervated mainly by the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve, C2-C3 spinal nerves and cervical sympathetic fibers. Facial nerve branches do not innervate it.

rationales.a: Trigeminal divisions provide major sensory innervation to cranial dura.
rationales.b: C2–C3 spinal nerves supply parts of the dura, especially posterior fossa.
rationales.c: Cervical sympathetic fibers accompany dural vessels; facial-nerve branches are not the source-listed dural supply.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q005.takeaway: The anterior cranial fossa dura receives branches from all three trigeminal divisions.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q005.displayText: The dura of the anterior cranial fossa receives supply from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve. The source lists anterior/posterior ethmoidal nerves from V1, nervus meningeus medius from V2, and nervus spinosus from V3.

rationales.b: The middle cranial fossa is supplied by V2/V3-associated meningeal branches rather than all three divisions.
rationales.c: Posterior-fossa dura is supplied chiefly by upper cervical and other listed posterior branches.
rationales.d: The foramen-magnum region is not the dural territory supplied by all three trigeminal divisions.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q006.takeaway: Posterior-fossa dura receives C2–C3 fibers carried through CN X and XII.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q006.displayText: The dura of the posterior cranial fossa is mainly supplied by C2 and C3 fibers distributed via cranial nerves X and XII. Therefore C2-C3 via vagus and hypoglossal nerves is correct for the marked region.

rationales.b: Ethmoidal nerves are V1 branches supplying anterior-fossa dura.
rationales.c: Nervus meningeus medius and nervus spinosus are V2/V3-associated branches supplying the middle fossa.
rationales.d: CN VII and IX are not the source-described C2–C3 route for posterior cranial-fossa dura.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q007.takeaway: The meningeal branch of the internal carotid supplies anterior, not posterior, cranial-fossa dura.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q007.displayText: The meningeal branch of the internal carotid artery does not supply the posterior cranial fossa; it contributes to anterior cranial fossa dura. The source lists ethmoidal/ICA branches for anterior fossa, middle/accessory meningeal and related branches for middle fossa, and occipital, vertebral and meningohypophyseal-derived branches for posterior fossa.

rationales.a: The source lists the middle meningeal artery among branches supplying anterior-fossa dura.
rationales.b: Accessory meningeal branches of the maxillary artery supply middle-fossa dura.
rationales.d: Meningeal branches of anterior/posterior ethmoidal arteries supply anterior-fossa dura; the keyed mismatch is ICA branch assigned to posterior fossa.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q008.takeaway: Meckel cave is an evagination of the lower tentorial layer at the petrous apex.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q008.displayText: Meckel's cave is an evagination of the lower layer of the tentorium cerebelli at the petrous apex. It is a dural recess in the middle cranial fossa that houses the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion and proximal trigeminal rootlets.
emphasis: lower layer of the tentorium cerebelli

rationales.a: Falx cerebelli is a separate dural fold and does not form Meckel cave.
rationales.b: Meckel cave is at the petrous apex from tentorium, not an evagination of falx cerebri.
rationales.c: Diaphragma sellae roofs the hypophyseal fossa and is not the trigeminal-ganglion recess.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q009.takeaway: The sigmoid sinus continues from the transverse sinus and drains to the internal jugular vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q009.displayText: The marked sinus is the sigmoid sinus, which continues from the transverse sinus. It follows an S-shaped groove near the mastoid, receives mastoid and condylar emissary veins, the venous plexus of the hypoglossal canal, inferior cerebellar veins and other tributaries, and joins the inferior petrosal sinus to form the internal jugular vein. Sigmoid/lateral sinus thrombosis can complicate ear or mastoid infection.

rationales.a: The sigmoid sinus receives blood from the transverse sinus rather than draining from it; flow proceeds transverse to sigmoid.
rationales.c: Inferior petrosal sinus joins the sigmoid/internal jugular drainage near the jugular bulb; it is not the upstream source shown.
rationales.d: Straight sinus drains into the confluence/transverse sinus pathway, not directly into the marked sigmoid sinus as keyed.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q010.takeaway: Abducens nerve lies next to the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q010.displayText: The abducens nerve is affected first because it runs within the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery. Oculomotor, trochlear and ophthalmic trigeminal fibers lie in the lateral wall and tend to be affected later. The maxillary division runs below the cavernous sinus rather than within it.

rationales.a: Trochlear nerve runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not adjacent to the internal carotid within it.
rationales.c: Ophthalmic division lies in the lateral wall and is generally affected after the intracavernous abducens nerve.
rationales.d: Maxillary division courses below the cavernous sinus and is not the first nerve affected by an intracavernous carotid aneurysm.

marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q011.takeaway: Deep middle cerebral vein is not a cavernous-sinus tributary; it contributes to the basal vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH18_Q011.displayText: The presentation suggests cavernous sinus thrombosis. The deep middle cerebral vein is not a tributary; it joins other deep cerebral veins to form the basal vein. Tributaries of the cavernous sinus include superior/inferior ophthalmic veins, sphenoparietal sinus, superficial middle cerebral vein and inferior cerebral vein. The source also lists drainage routes and contents including the cavernous ICA, sympathetic plexus, abducens nerve and lateral-wall cranial nerves.

rationales.a: Sphenoparietal sinus drains to the cavernous sinus and is a listed tributary.
rationales.c: Middle meningeal venous channels/sinus are included among cavernous-sinus tributaries in the source item.
rationales.d: Inferior ophthalmic vein drains to the cavernous sinus.
